title: Everyday Magic
subtitle: Stars Between the Strings · Chapter 34 of 40
content:
The coffee tasted right.

I should have been suspicious.

Greg leaned against the kitchen counter, pretending he hadn't been watching my face as I took the first sip.

"Well?"

"Did you remember how I like it?"

"No."

"Greg."

"Okay, maybe I wrote it down once."

I turned toward the fridge. A small square of paper was held up by a magnet shaped like a guitar. Beside the grocery list, in his uneven handwriting, were three words: *Jasper's coffee. Remember.*

I smiled.

"You're ridiculous."

"Professionally."

The toast was burning.

We saved half of it.

It was a weekday morning in Beach City, ordinary enough that the light through the blinds seemed almost too dramatic for the circumstances. A towel hung over the back of a chair. The washing machine made a noise we'd been avoiding for three days. On the table sat a list of things neither of us wanted to do.

Greg stared at the list.

"Could we just stay here and admire how good we are at making breakfast?"

"Only if the laundry does itself."

He sighed.

Greg wrote the tasks on the back of an old set list. Every third item was either underlined twice or surrounded by an enormous question mark.

"That's not a system," I said.

"That's art."

"Then why does the washing machine have three exclamation points?"

"Because it sounds like a drummer trying to escape."

I had to admit he was right.

The calendar on the wall still showed the day we'd gone to Lanternweald together to watch the Starwake lights come on. Greg had drawn a small guitar beside it, then forgotten to erase the reminder when we returned.

"Do you ever feel like you have to choose one place to call home?" I asked.

He looked at the calendar.

"Sometimes. The van was home for a long time because it could leave whenever I needed it to."

"And now?"

"Now I want places where I can stay without deciding I'm stuck. That feels different."

I rested my hand on the counter.

"I want that too. But it's going to take practice when our schedules overlap."

He nodded.

"Maybe the next thing on the list should be to ask each other before promising the whole day to somebody."

"That's a reasonable thing to write."

He added it in enormous letters.

I looked at him.

"Not a guitar drawing?"

"Don't rush genius."

Then he drew a guitar anyway.

We divided the work without treating it as a grand agreement. He would call the repair shop about the washing machine. I would take the recycling to the collection point and check the schedule for my next Threadway crossing. We would both go grocery shopping because neither trusted the other to remember everything on the list.

"That last part feels insulting," he said.

"You bought three jars of mustard last week."

"It was on sale."

"We still have two unopened."

"An investment."

I laughed.

The day unraveled by noon.

The repair shop could not come until Tuesday. The collection point closed early because a delivery had blocked the street. One of the grocery items had been marked incorrectly on the shelf, and the clerk needed to check the price before we paid.

None of these things was remotely tragic.

Greg behaved as though they were part of an elaborate comedy written specifically to embarrass him.

At the register, I watched him reach for his wallet to pay for everything. I stopped him.

"We said we'd split this."

"I know. I just—"

"Want to be generous?"

"Yeah."

"You can. But asking me whether I'd like you to cover it is different from deciding I can't contribute."

He looked at the groceries.

"Right. Sorry."

"Can we try again?"

He handed me the lighter bag.

"Would you like to take this one and cover the vegetables?"

"Yes."

The clerk waited patiently while we sorted it out.

Back home, Greg offered to fix the loose shelf before lunch. I told him we could wait until we had the proper brackets, then put the dry goods in the lower cabinet so the shelf wasn't carrying weight it couldn't hold.

He looked at the empty space.

"I was hoping to be the hero of one household repair today."

"You can be the hero of calling the washing-machine technician."

"That's a terrible hero origin."

I kissed his cheek.

"The best ones are."

We ate sandwiches on the porch and watched Steven pass by on his way to meet friends. He stopped long enough to borrow a clean cloth for an art project and returned it before supper.

Greg watched him leave with a soft expression.

"He's got his own plans."

"Yes."

"I used to get worried when I didn't know every detail."

"Do you still?"

"Sometimes. Not as much."

I leaned against the railing.

"That's how I want us to be, too."

He looked at me.

"How?"

"Two people with a life together and other lives of their own. I'm ethically non-monogamous, and I prefer polyamory. You know that. I don't want you guessing that every time I make plans with someone else, I'm taking something from you."

He considered.

"I don't always like missing you."

"You're allowed to miss me."

"Can I ask for Thursday evening?"

"Yes, unless the archive meeting runs long. I'll tell you early if it changes."

He smiled.

"That's an actual plan."

"Shocking, isn't it?"

We finished lunch and walked down to the shore. The sky had turned pale grey. Greg brought the blanket with the old patch. We didn't need it, but he insisted it was part of his beach identity.

At the water, he asked whether I'd like to dance.

"There's no music."

"I'm a musician. I can supply it."

He hummed an intentionally terrible tune and held out his hand.

I took it.

We moved together in the sand until we were laughing too hard to keep the rhythm. He stopped and looked at me, his expression suddenly tender.

"Can I kiss you?"

"Yes."

The kiss was warm, unhurried, and made my heart feel much less interested in the list still waiting at home.

Later we returned to the kitchen, wrote down the repair appointment, and ate dinner with the good plates despite having no particular reason to celebrate.

The washing machine still made its noise.

The grocery list was already half unfinished again.

But Greg had remembered the coffee, I'd remembered the vegetables, and neither of us had to pretend ordinary days were beneath the kind of love we wanted.

He drew a tiny guitar beside Thursday on the calendar. I left it there.

On Thursday, the laundry technician arrived with a replacement belt and a bill that made Greg whistle.

"Could I have fixed it myself?" he asked.

"Probably not safely with the tools you have," the technician replied. "And the old belt was about to damage the drum."

Greg looked at me.

"Another dramatic rescue prevented by paying someone."

"I know. Terrible for your reputation."

He laughed.

We kept the repair receipt with the other household records rather than pretending the machine would never fail again. Greg set a reminder to check the filter on the schedule the technician recommended.

That evening we cooked together. He chopped vegetables while I handled the stove, and we argued over whether an old song counted as dinner music if we both knew it by heart.

He hummed a few bars of something original instead, deliberately missing a note to make me laugh.

When I turned from the counter, he was watching me with a warmth that made the kitchen feel smaller.

"Would you like to go out?" he asked.

"Right now?"

"Just a walk. No audience. No heroic repairs."

I took his hand.

"Yes."

We left the repaired machine humming softly behind us and went to see whether the sea was still there. It was.
